results.question_title: [FEAT] Fast API Middleware in Routers

vector.answer:
The sections show FastAPI already has a mechanism for exactly the use case you describe: dependencies attached at router and application level, so shared logic like authentication or database access is written once rather than on every route.

You can pass dependencies when including a router:

    app.include_router(admin.router, prefix="/admin", tags=["admin"], dependencies=[Depends(get_token_header)], responses={418: {"description": "I'm a teapot"}})

And you can declare global dependencies on the app itself, which are combined with the dependencies of each APIRouter:

    app = FastAPI(dependencies=[Depends(get_query_token)])

APIRouter is described as a mini FastAPI class that supports all the same options, including parameters, responses, dependencies and tags, and a router can be included in another router with router.include_router(other_router), so the shared behaviour composes down a tree.

What the sections do not cover: any middleware or extension hook on APIRouter, and any after response hook equivalent to your after_request. They document dependencies only, not a before/after request extension API.

graph.answer:
FastAPI already has this: router-level dependencies. You do not need a new extension mechanism for shared work like authentication or getting a database handle.

Put them on the APIRouter itself, alongside prefix, tags and responses:

router = APIRouter(prefix="/items", tags=["items"], dependencies=[Depends(get_token_header)], responses={...})

They are added to every path operation in that router and are executed and solved for each request made to them. The docs point this out explicitly as the way to require authentication for a whole group of path operations.

If the router is shared and you cannot modify it, pass the same parameters at inclusion time instead, which leaves the original untouched:

app.include_router(admin.router, prefix="/admin", tags=["admin"], dependencies=[Depends(get_token_header)], responses={418: {...}})

For the whole app: FastAPI(dependencies=[Depends(get_query_token)]).

Execution order is router dependencies first, then dependencies in the path operation decorator, then normal parameter dependencies; dependencies declared on an individual path operation still run too.

The sections do not describe any after_request or response-side hook, so the after_request half of your proposed Extension is not covered here.

results.question_title: Feature Request: Allow route return types to be FileResponse | JSONResponse

vector.answer:
The sections show two documented ways to do this today.

First, set response_model=None. This makes FastAPI skip response model generation, so you can keep any return type annotation you need without it affecting the application, which is exactly the case shown in the docs:

    @app.get("/portal", response_model=None)
    async def get_portal(teleport: bool = False) -> Response | dict:

That removes the need for the # type: ignore comments while keeping FileResponse | JSONResponse in the signature.

Second, if you do not need the union in the annotation, annotate the return as Response. FastAPI handles that automatically because the annotation is the Response class or a subclass of it, and type checkers are satisfied since the concrete response classes are subclasses of Response.

For the OpenAPI side, the docs show returning a FileResponse directly from a path operation and declaring the extra media type with the responses parameter, for example responses={200: {"content": {"image/png": {}}, "description": "Return the JSON item or an image."}}, so both outcomes are documented.

The documented pattern for exactly this case is to return the Response directly and not declare it as the return type.

When you return a Response such as JSONResponse from a path operation, it is returned directly: it will not be serialized with a model, so you set content and status_code yourself. That is the documented mechanism for emitting additional status codes, and the docs example that does it declares no return annotation on the function. FileResponse works the same way when returned directly; alternatively you can set response_class=FileResponse on the decorator and return the file path from the function.

The reason the annotation fights you is that a declared return type is a response model: FastAPI uses it to serialize your data to JSON with Pydantic, and returns the JSON bytes with an application/json media type directly. results.question_title: Unexpected Behavior with Aliased Query Parameters in FastAPI

vector.answer:
This is the intended behavior. From the alias documentation: when you declare an alias, "that alias is what will be used to find the parameter value." So alias='employee_name' makes employee_name the name FastAPI reads from the query string. emp_name is only the Python variable name that receives the value; it stops being the name clients send.

That is why /employee/?emp_name=apple falls into the else branch: nothing named employee_name was sent, the parameter takes its default of None, and `if emp_name` is false. /employee/?employee_name=apple supplies the value, so the if branch runs.

The rationale given in the docs is that the external parameter name often cannot be a Python variable name. Their example wants item-query in the URL; the closest legal Python name is item_query, so you write q: Annotated[str | None, Query(alias="item-query")] = None and the alias is what is looked up. The alias replaces the public name rather than adding a second accepted spelling.

vector.answer:
The sections explain the cause but not the feature request.

Cause: FastAPI dependencies with `yield` are turned into context managers internally. "Any function that is valid to use with `@contextlib.contextmanager` or `@contextlib.asynccontextmanager` would be valid to use as a FastAPI dependency. In fact, FastAPI uses those two decorators internally." The docs also say: "Make sure to use `yield` one single time per dependency." Your `get_thingy` catches the exception from `open_file` and returns without ever yielding, so contextlib raises `RuntimeError: generator didn't yield`.

The docs name this pattern directly: if you catch an exception with `except` in a dependency with `yield` and do not raise it again (or raise a new exception), FastAPI cannot notice there was an exception, the client gets a 500, and "the server will not have any logs or any other indication of what was the error." The fix per the docs is to re-raise (or raise a new exception, e.g. `HTTPException`) rather than swallowing it, so the real error surfaces.

The sections say nothing about FastAPI catching this RuntimeError itself or naming the responsible dependency.

Your code is not what the docs currently show. In the documented example, the `RequestValidationError` handler does not stringify the exception; it iterates the errors and builds a message:

```python
@app.exception_handler(RequestValidationError)
async def validation_exception_handler(request, exc: RequestValidationError):
    message = "Validation errors:"
    for error in exc.errors():
        message += f"\nField: {error['loc']}, Error: {error['msg']}"
    return PlainTextResponse(message, status_code=400)
```

Your version uses `PlainTextResponse(str(exc), ...)`, so the body is the stringified error list you saw. It is still returned as a plain text response, it just contains the raw repr of `exc` rather than a formatted message.

The docs give the reason for the loop: `RequestValidationError` carries the file name and line where the validation error happened, so converting it to a string and returning it directly could leak information about your system. That is why the example extracts and shows each error independently. Use the loop form and `curl http://localhost:8000/items/foo` will return the `Validation errors:` text.

    @app.get("/items/stream", response_class=EventSourceResponse)

        start = last_event_id + 1 if last_event_id is not None else 0
        for i, item in enumerate(items):
            if i < start:
                continue
            yield ServerSentEvent(data=item, id=str(i))

results.question_title: Cannot use Body (pydantic schemas)  and file upload together in an API

vector.answer:
This is expected, and it is an HTTP constraint rather than a FastAPI one. The docs warn that you can declare multiple File and Form parameters in a path operation, but you cannot also declare Body fields that you expect to receive as JSON, because the request body will be encoded as multipart/form-data instead of application/json. Your create_xp: EgSchemas is a JSON body field, so a multipart request carrying the file has no JSON body for it and you get 422 Unprocessable Entity.

Send everything as form data instead, declaring the model's fields as Form parameters next to the file:

from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import FastAPI, File, Form, UploadFile

@app.post("/")
async def example(
    name: Annotated[str, Form()],
    age: Annotated[int, Form()],
    file: Annotated[UploadFile, File()],
):
    return {"message": "Success", "filename": file.filename}

The files and form fields then arrive together as form data, and you can declare some files as bytes and some as UploadFile. File() also accepts metadata such as description when used with UploadFile.

results.question_title: how to add a non-blocking endpoint that calls an awaitable function but can't await it

vector.answer:
Use BackgroundTasks. Declare a background_tasks: BackgroundTasks parameter on the path operation and hand it the function plus its arguments instead of awaiting it, then return right away:

from fastapi import BackgroundTasks, FastAPI

@app.post("/deal")
async def deal(waiting: float, background_tasks: BackgroundTasks):
    background_tasks.add_task(slow, waiting)
    return {"message": "started in the background"}

You pass the function object and its arguments, so there is no un-awaited coroutine and no RuntimeWarning. The docs state the task function "can be an async def or normal def function, FastAPI will know how to handle it correctly", so you do not need to wrap the third party call in subprocess.Popen.

One fix to your slow(): the docs define the task with a normal def when the work does not use async and await. Your slow() uses blocking time.sleep and a blocking third party library, so declare it def slow(waiting: float), not async def.

The sections shown do not state whether two background tasks from two requests execute concurrently, so I cannot confirm that part from them.

results.question_title: How does StreamingResponse work?

vector.answer:
From the sections, the documented pattern is: declare `response_class=StreamingResponse` on the path operation, then `yield` each chunk from the path operation function itself. FastAPI hands each yielded chunk to the `StreamingResponse` as is: it will not convert it to JSON, will not run it through Pydantic, and will not serialize it in any way.

Example from the docs:

    @app.get("/story/stream", response_class=StreamingResponse)
    async def stream_story() -> AsyncIterable[str]:
        for line in message.splitlines():
            yield line

The return type annotation is optional here. Because FastAPI does not serialize the data, the annotation is only for your editor and tools; it is not used by FastAPI. The docs state this leaves you with "the freedom and responsibility" to produce and encode the exact bytes you want sent.

On your second question: the sections do not mention `stream_response`, and they do not document the constructor form in your example (passing a generator to `StreamingResponse(...)` and returning it). I cannot describe the internals of how the generator is consumed from what is provided here.
vector.reason: Conveys the maintainer's mechanism, that each yielded chunk is streamed to the client as is without serialization, even though it declines to describe the internal consumption of the generator.

graph.answer:
`StreamingResponse` takes an async generator or a normal generator/iterator (a function with `yield`) and streams the response body from it. Each value the generator yields is sent as one chunk. FastAPI hands each chunk to the response as is, it does not convert it to JSON or anything else, which is why your example yields raw bytes.

One caveat the docs call out: an async task can only be cancelled when it reaches an `await`. Your `fake_video_streamer` has no `await`, so it cannot be cancelled properly and may keep running after cancellation is requested. The docs' version of your exact example adds `await anyio.sleep(0)` after the yield to give the event loop a chance to handle cancellation. This matters more with large or infinite streams.

The recommended style is not to return `StreamingResponse` directly. Instead declare `response_class=StreamingResponse` on the path operation and `yield` each chunk from the path operation function itself, which handles cancellation for you. For JSON items, yield them and declare a return type like `AsyncIterable[Item]`.

The sections do not cover FastAPI's internal `stream_response` function, so I can't describe it.

results.question_title: set_cookie straight up broken

vector.answer:
Not a bug. The problem is that you set the cookie on the injected `response` parameter but then return a `PlainTextResponse` directly.

The docs describe two distinct mechanisms:

1. `Response` parameter: you declare `response: Response`, set cookies on that temporary object, and then return a normal object (a dict, a model, etc.). FastAPI uses that temporary response to extract the cookies, headers, and status code and puts them into the final response it builds around your returned value.

2. Returning a `Response` directly: you create the response yourself, set the cookies on that object, and return it.

The docs warn explicitly: "if you return a response directly instead of using the `Response` parameter, FastAPI will return it directly." Your `PlainTextResponse` is returned as is, so the temporary `response` object you set the cookie on is never used, and no `Set-Cookie` header reaches the browser.

Fix it either way: build the `PlainTextResponse` first and call `set_cookie` on it before returning it, or drop the explicit response and return plain content so FastAPI merges the cookie from the `Response` parameter.
vector.reason: Gives the maintainer's key fact, that a directly returned Response is used as the final response so the injected Response object with the cookie is ignored.

graph.answer:
This is not a bug, it's the interaction between the two features you're combining.

The `Response` parameter is a *temporary* response object. FastAPI extracts the cookies (and headers and status code) you set on it and puts them into the final response that it builds from the value you returned. That works when you return a normal object, such as a `dict` or a database model, and let FastAPI construct the response.

You are not doing that. You return a `PlainTextResponse`, and when you return a `Response` or any subclass of it directly, FastAPI passes it directly: no data conversion, no `response_model` filtering, nothing. That returned response is the one sent to the browser, and it is not the temporary object you called `set_cookie` on, so your cookie never gets merged in. That also matches your finding that setting the header manually works.

Two ways forward, per the sections: return a plain value (a `dict`, for example) and keep using the `Response` parameter, or build the `PlainTextResponse` yourself and set the cookie on that object before returning it. results.question_title: @app.middleware("http") wrong execution order

vector.answer:
This is by design, and it is documented. From the middleware docs:

"When you add multiple middlewares using either `@app.middleware()` decorator or `app.add_middleware()` method, each new middleware wraps the application, forming a stack. The last middleware added is the *outermost*, and the first is the *innermost*. On the request path, the *outermost* middleware runs first. On the response path, it runs last."

So in your code `test1` is added first (innermost) and `test2` second (outermost). Request order is test2 -> test1 -> route, and response order is route -> test1 -> test2. That is exactly the output you are seeing.

The docs give the same example with `add_middleware`:

    app.add_middleware(MiddlewareA)
    app.add_middleware(MiddlewareB)

    Request:  MiddlewareB -> MiddlewareA -> route
    Response: route -> MiddlewareA -> MiddlewareB

Both registration styles behave identically here, and the docs describe this stacking as what "ensures that middlewares are executed in a predictable and controllable order." If you want `test1` to run first on the request path, register it last.
vector.reason: Reproduces the maintainer's stacking rule, last middleware added is outermost and runs first on the request path, with the correct order for the user's code.

Any function that would be valid to use with those decorators is already valid as a FastAPI dependency in its undecorated form.

So drop `@asynccontextmanager` and pass the plain async generator:

    async def get_hi():
        try:
            yield 'hi'
        finally:
            print('finally')

Because you decorated it, `Depends(get_hi)` calls the decorated callable and receives the `_AsyncGeneratorContextManager` object, which is exactly what you printed.

If you have an existing context manager you want to reuse, the documented pattern is to enter it inside a dependency with `yield`, using `with` or `async with`, and yield the value from there.

Because `c: int` is a singular type, FastAPI interprets it as a query parameter, not as a key in the request body. The rules the docs give for function parameters are: a parameter also declared in the path is a path parameter; a parameter of a singular type (`int`, `float`, `str`, `bool`, etc.) is a query parameter; a parameter typed as a Pydantic model is the request body. So your endpoint expects the body to be the `A` object and `c` to arrive as `?c=...`.

To get the JSON shape you want, tell FastAPI to treat `c` as another body key using `Body`:

```python
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Body, FastAPI

@app.post("/test")
async def test(a: A, c: Annotated[int, Body()]):
    return {"a": a, "c": c}
```

The docs show this pattern producing exactly that nested body, with each body parameter as a top-level key alongside the model objects. `Body` also accepts the same extra validation and metadata parameters as `Query` and `Path`.

They already are required, with no extra configuration. The rule is that a model attribute is required unless it has a default value: "when a model attribute has a default value, it is not required. Otherwise, it is required. Use None to make it just optional."

Your Bird model declares name: str, wingspan: int and speed: float with no defaults, so all three are required and will appear as required in the generated openapi.json. A payload of {'name': ..., 'speed': ...} is therefore already invalid against the schema, and the validation Pydantic performs under the hood will reject it.

A field only becomes optional when you give it a default, e.g. description: str | None = None. If some field of yours is showing up as not required, it is because it has a default value; remove the default and it becomes required.

The difference is that `Query` imported from `fastapi` is a function, not the marker object itself. The docs state: "When you import `Query`, `Path` and others from `fastapi`, they are actually functions. That when called, return instances of classes of the same name." So `Annotated[T, Query]` puts the *function* in the annotation, which is not the `Query` instance FastAPI looks for; every documented usage calls it, e.g. `Annotated[str | None, Query(max_length=50)]`.

Fix your alias by calling it:

```Python
GenericQuery = Annotated[Annotated[T, BeforeValidator(map_empty_to_null)], Query()]
```

On your other assumption: the docs say a parameter of a **singular type** (`int`, `float`, `str`, `bool`, ...) is interpreted as a query parameter, and only a Pydantic-model type is interpreted as a body, so `q: str | None = None` is a query parameter without any `Query`. `list[Foo] | None` is not a singular type, so it does not get that automatic treatment and needs the explicit `Query()` marker, which is why `foo` works and `bar` does not.

results.question_title: Why does pip install fastapi include a SKILL.md under .agents/skills/?

That file is FastAPI's official skill for AI coding agents. It is bundled inside the package deliberately, so its guidance stays aligned with the version of FastAPI installed in your project and updates when you update FastAPI.

uvx library-skills
